title: ANALYSIS | The 'unity' fight splitting Danielle Smith's party intensifies at UCP convention | CBC News
html:
Calgary·Analysis

The 'unity' fight splitting Danielle Smith's party intensifies at UCP convention

Inside the high-stakes battle to stack weekend's meeting and control party board

Loyalists to Premier Danielle Smith are spearheading massive get-out-the-vote efforts for this weekend’s UCP convention, in hopes of seizing firm control of the party board in the aftermath of Alberta’s separation referendum.

This includes offers to pay for meeting tickets and a surge of registrations by members from the party’s old Progressive Conservative wing, CBC News has learned.

On the other side, grassroots party activists are also spending money and organizing in hopes of electing more independence-friendly officials to the party board. But after several years of insurgent groups like Take Back Alberta holding sway at conventions, this could be the year that the party establishment strikes back.

“This is a similar effort that would happen for an actual leadership race,” one senior United Conservative told CBC News about the intensity of convention organizing.

However, Smith’s leadership isn’t up for a vote at this UCP annual general meeting, starting Friday in Calgary. It’s not the party president’s turn to be up for election either, but convention-goers will choose another eight of 18 voting directors on the UCP’s board, including chief financial officer and regional directors.

This weekend’s battle, insiders believe, could help tilt the board’s balance away from independence — or from the influence of Smith and her inner circle.

One party organizer trying to rally traditional Tories to the convention is Hal Danchilla, a lobbying firm partner who served as a key advisor to former premier Ralph Klein.

To explain his aims ahead of the convention, he hearkened back to the approach taken during the old Progressive Conservative dynasty, before its 2017 merger with the Wildrose Party to form the UCP.

“One of the fundamental pieces in the past was that we worked for the leader of the party,” Danchilla told CBC News. “The leader didn’t work for the party.”

At past UCP conventions, partisans have shown support for Smith. But they've also elected party board members that her loyalists are now trying to push out. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

How pitched are attempts to stack the convention, which a record 7,000 members are registered to attend?

One Tory in Calgary who hasn’t been active in the UCP told CBC News that of the many people who have urged her to attend this weekend, two separately offered to cover her registration fee, which after the early-bird discount runs $399.

The Tory, who spoke on the condition she not be named, declined the money, preferring to go on her own dime (and she wouldn’t say who offered). But the urgency got her concerned about the party’s health heading into next year’s provincial election.

“If you have to whip your own party like this at your own convention ... how are you going to run an election?” she said.

Multiple sources said the Smith loyalists’ goal is to bring thousands of supporters out to the convention, to outnumber activists’ efforts on the other side.

After 75 per cent of Albertans supported staying in Canada in the October referendum, the premier shifted from her long-standing tolerance for openly backing separatism within her UCP ranks.

She said she wants everyone speaking for her party to acknowledge and accept the referendum results, including all MLAs and election candidates next year. The party has issued a pledge for all board candidates and current riding association presidents to sign, saying they “abide by” that vote’s outcome — although several presidents have refused that demand.

New candidates for board posts include several UCPers who campaigned against a united Canada, including Chris Scott of the independence group Let’s Talk Alberta.

Other candidates have banded together on a slate dubbed Team Unity, including Patrick Malkin, a party vice-president whose day job is as the premier’s deputy chief of staff. This “team” professes loyalty to the premier and a commitment to a “strong Alberta within a United Canada.”

“It is eight like-minded, hard-working dedicated people who are running for the board that are unifying together,” Ken Engler, a candidate to be the party’s chief financial officer, said at a Calgary board candidates’ forum last week.

Part of an email sent to UCP members from board candidates calling themselves the party's 'Unity' slate. (United Conservative Party/CBC news graphic illustration)

The banner on this group’s campaign emails features the premier’s photo, but Smith has not endorsed any candidates.

“While the premier is not involved or associated with the creation of this group, it is great to see individual members from across our province organizing to keep our party united,” Smith spokesperson Ryan Fournier said in an email.

On Wednesday, a group of 21 Calgary business and community leaders sent party members a letter endorsing the slate's eight candidates to keep the "UCP strong and unified." It was co-ordinated by lawyer and veteran conservative fundraiser Brian Felesky, who said he backs Smith's efforts to "put the whole issue of separation to rest."

"I firmly believe in a united Canada, a united Alberta, and I don’t want this AGM to be hijacked," said another signatory, former Calgary police commission chair Mike Shaikh.

Not only is this slate taking on some of the pro-independence challengers like Scott — who willingly signed the post-referendum pledge — but it’s also running candidates against a few current directors with ties to the independence cause, including regional directors Brad LaForge and Mark Hunt, and CFO Jack Redekop.

“I don't need to be the establishment's choice, but I want to be your choice,” LaForge told the Calgary forum last Friday.

“I'm asking you to vote for the kind of party we can be, one where respect matters more than influence — where unity is something we build together, not something we demand from one another.”

The “unity” slate has also rankled the party’s board president, Rob Smith. In a social media post on Tuesday, he said it’s “extremely offensive” to suggest that other candidates aren’t for unity, and announced he’d endorse three contenders running against Team Unity members.

Danchilla’s view of the party working for the leader and not vice versa runs counter to the perspective of many UCP grassroots activists who prefer more of a bottom-up approach.

“The party doesn’t exist so that the leadership can use it to accomplish their goals,” Scott told CBC News this week. “The membership is supposed to be operating the party to make the leader and the government accomplish their goal.”

The party’s board will have particular importance with 2027 Alberta election looming. It holds influence over the UCP’s multimillion-dollar war chest and candidate selection, among other political matters.

Several current directors like LaForge and Hunt joined the board with the backing of activist groups like David Parker’s Take Back Alberta and Mitch Sylvestre’s pro-independence Alberta Prosperity Project, which sought to exert more heavy influence on the party and UCP government by controlling the board.

As those groups gained power at party conventions, those from the Tory side retreated or stopped coming. In the first post-referendum convention, there’s a big effort to bring them back into the fold to preserve the UCP as a staunchly federalist (and anti-separatist) party.

Elan MacDonald has helped reach out to hundreds of Tories and UCPers, urging them to come to the AGM. She was deputy chief of staff to former Tory premiers Ed Stelmach and Alison Redford — both of whom Danielle Smith opposed as Wildrose leader — but has emerged recently as a Smith backer, hosting a coffee party for the premier at her Edmonton house last July. MacDonald recently left a University of Alberta job to become a government-relations consultant.

“Conservatives are re-engaging with the UCP for this AGM because they see a small sliver of conservatives dictating an agenda that we don't share,” MacDonald said.

“We need a board that is very clear that this is not a separatist party. This is a broad-based conservative party that has broad-based conservative values.”

Elan MacDonald served as a key aide for two former Tory premiers, and is currently in government relations. (flyyeg.com)

Danchilla, who is working with MacDonald’s team, said the group is not offering to pay convention-goers. CBC was unable to confirm the identities of any organizations or individuals who are offering to cover costs of those intending to support the Unity slate.

On the other side of this board election battle, a pro-independence group named Next Step Alberta is offering to cover half the convention fees for like-minded supporters. Next Step head Nathan Steinke said he’s been getting referrals from APP to provide the subsidies to conservatives who bought their own tickets.

“I think that sovereignty-minded people need to be represented,” Steinke said. He’s a former UCP cabinet aide and is married to Samantha Steinke, a veteran party board member who he says has accompanied him to some events where he’s touted his project.

Sylvestre, who has told APP backers he wants to get 1,000 of them to the convention, confirmed Nathan Steinke’s group is supporting him, and said repaying ticket-holders is “completely aboveboard.”

While party members must register individually for the AGM, the rules do not prohibit covering others’ costs, party spokesperson Dave Prisco said in an email.

Nathan Steinke said his budget for the effort is modest — under $15,000 — and he’s so far financially supported fewer than 100 AGM attendees.

He said he’s worried about what happens to the UCP if independence activists are shut out from the board and separatists don’t feel they have a home in the party.

“You know, if the establishment basically rolls in … and just steamrolls us, then I think that they are in some ways damaging unity more than sovereignty ever could,” Steinke said.

'Canada Guy' stages a small counter-protest at an October independence rally at the Alberta legislature. UCP Leader Danielle Smith has urged her party to stop talking about separatism. (Amanda May Erickson/The Canadian Press)

Chris Scott, who is confident he has enough supporters to get elected as the party’s central region director, echoed this sentiment

“If the rural and the grassroots folks smell funny business, that’s going to be reflected in the election,” he said.

“I think the party has to be really careful about the image they portray to the members, because there’s a lot of members that already feel disenfranchised.”

Concern about the next election and the UCP’s reputation is very much on the minds of many key party figures. The NDP’s byelection win in a former safe Calgary seat in September surprised organizers throughout the UCP, and party president Rob Smith told one podcast recently about the lesson it sent.

“What our door-knockers are hearing, not just in the official Calgary-Shaw byelection, but in door-knocking that’s happening across the province: there are an awful lot of Albertans who believe the UCP is a separatist party,” he told the show Unfiltered earlier this month.

Some in the party are bidding to deputize several hundred or thousand convention attendees to help dispel that image, and notch a comfortable win for Danielle Smith in her final convention before next October’s election.

with files from Alex Boyd
summary: Premier's loyalists and pro-independence activists campaigning for control of party's influential board of directors.
